instagram_caption:
Kubrick's candlelit film used lenses built for the moon. 🕯️

In 1975 Stanley Kubrick made Barry Lyndon and insisted its castle interiors be lit the way they were in the 1700s: candles only, no fill light. Film stock of the day could barely see in the dark, so he went hunting for the fastest lens ever made.

Zeiss had built just ten Planar 50mm f/0.7 lenses for NASA's Apollo program. Six went to NASA. Kubrick bought three. Executive producer Jan Harlan says he picked up the first one himself in Oberkochen in 1972. The catch: the rear glass sat a few millimetres from the film, and Zeiss told him it would never fit a movie camera. Kubrick had a Mitchell BNC cut apart until it did.

On set the candles had three wicks each, the whole film was pushed a stop in development, and focus was so thin a video camera watched the actors from the side with a grid drawn on the monitor.

It won four Oscars, including cinematography, and still failed to cover its costs in America. Today directors rank it the twelfth greatest film ever made. And the lenses built to photograph the moon? Zeiss itself now says there is no evidence they ever did. Their famous pictures are of candles.

Candlelight or studio lights? 👇
